  // ── Lesson 7.4: Concept Exercise (NEW Essential Production OTP Pattern) ────
  {
    id: 'ch07-l04',
    chapterNumber: 7,
    lessonNumber: 4,
    lessonType: 'concept_exercise',
    title: 'Async Worker Offloading with gen_server:reply/2 & Process Hibernation',
    difficulty: 'Intermediate',
    conceptMarkdown: `## Why This Matters in Production

A \`gen_server\` process handles messages from its mailbox strictly one at a time. This guarantees that your state map is never subject to concurrent data races.
However, this serial execution model introduces a severe architectural danger: **Head-of-Line (HoL) Blocking**.

Imagine an analytics coordinator server:
1. Client A calls \`generate_report(Server, "report_monthly")\`, which requires heavy computational aggregation taking **500ms**.
2. While the server is executing that 500ms computation inside \`handle_call/3\`, Clients B, C, and D submit fast requests: \`get_completed_count(Server)\` (which takes **0.01ms**).
3. **Clients B, C, and D are frozen waiting in the mailbox!** Fast queries experience unacceptable latency spikes solely because a slow job blocked the server thread.

Erlang solves this elegant design challenge with **\`gen_server:reply/2\`**!

## Deep Concept Breakdown & Under the Hood

### Unblocking the Server: \`{noreply, State}\` + \`gen_server:reply/2\`

Look closely at the arguments of \`handle_call/3\`:
\`\`\`erlang
handle_call(Request, From, State)
\`\`\`
What is \`From\`?
As we discovered in Chapter 6 (Lesson 6.8), \`From\` is the tuple \`{ClientPid, MonitorRefTag}\`!
Usually, your callback returns \`{reply, Reply, NewState}\`, and the \`gen_server\` engine immediately sends the reply to \`From\`.

However, OTP provides an alternative:
1. When a heavy request arrives, you **do not compute it inside \`handle_call\`**.
2. Instead, you spawn a disposable helper worker process and pass \`From\` to that worker.
3. Your \`handle_call\` immediately returns **\`{noreply, UpdatedState}\`**!

\`\`\`erlang
handle_call({generate_report, JobId, ComputeFun}, From, State = #{in_flight := InFlight}) ->
    ServerSelf = self(),
    spawn(fun() ->
        Result = ComputeFun(),
        %% 1. Worker directly unblocks waiting client via From tag!
        gen_server:reply(From, {ok, JobId, Result}),
        %% 2. Worker informs coordinator of completion
        ServerSelf ! {job_finished, JobId}
    end),
    %% Server loop returns in 2 microseconds!
    {noreply, State#{in_flight := InFlight + 1}}.
\`\`\`

Because \`handle_call/3\` returned \`{noreply, ...}\` in **2 microseconds**, the \`gen_server\` is immediately free to answer incoming fast queries from Clients B, C, and D! Meanwhile, Client A remains paused in its synchronous \`call\` until the background worker delivers the answer directly via \`gen_server:reply(From, ...)\`.

### Process Hibernation: \`hibernate\`

In large-scale systems (like chat servers with 1,000,000 connected rooms or background workers waiting between cron sweeps), thousands of processes sit idle for minutes or hours. Even an idle BEAM process occupies memory for its heap, stack, and reduction tables.

When an actor is idle, returning \`hibernate\` as the 4th element of a return tuple:
\`\`\`erlang
{reply, Reply, NewState, hibernate}
%% or
{noreply, NewState, hibernate}
\`\`\`
instructs the BEAM VM to:
1. Run an immediate, aggressive full-sweep garbage collection.
2. Discard the call stack.
3. Compact the heap into a single contiguous block of minimal memory (~300 bytes).
4. Put the process into deep hibernation until the next message arrives in its mailbox!

When a new message arrives, the BEAM automatically wakes the process without any special handling in your code.

> [!warning] Production OTP Trap: Forgetting to Reply from the Spawned Worker
> If you spawn a worker to handle a call and that worker crashes or exits before calling \`gen_server:reply(From, ...)\`, the client process will hang until its 5,000ms call timeout expires! In production, wrap the worker computation in \`try...catch\` to guarantee that \`gen_server:reply(From, {error, worker_crashed})\` is always invoked.

## Parallel Worked Example

The following image processor coordinator demonstrates async worker offloading with \`gen_server:reply/2\`:

\`\`\`erlang
-module(image_coordinator).
-behaviour(gen_server).
-export([start_link/0, resize_image/3, get_metrics/1, sleep_idle/1, stop/1]).
-export([init/1, handle_call/3, handle_cast/2, handle_info/2, terminate/2, code_change/3]).

start_link() -> gen_server:start_link(?MODULE, [], []).
resize_image(Pid, ImgId, ResizeFun) -> gen_server:call(Pid, {resize, ImgId, ResizeFun}, 5000).
get_metrics(Pid) -> gen_server:call(Pid, get_metrics).
sleep_idle(Pid) -> gen_server:call(Pid, sleep_idle).
stop(Pid) -> gen_server:stop(Pid).

init([]) -> {ok, #{active => 0, done => 0}}.

handle_call({resize, ImgId, ResizeFun}, From, State = #{active := Active}) ->
    Self = self(),
    spawn(fun() ->
        Res = ResizeFun(),
        gen_server:reply(From, {ok, ImgId, Res}),
        Self ! {task_done, ImgId}
    end),
    {noreply, State#{active := Active + 1}};
handle_call(get_metrics, _From, State = #{active := A, done := D}) ->
    {reply, #{active => A, done => D}, State};
handle_call(sleep_idle, _From, State) ->
    {reply, sleeping, State, hibernate}.

handle_cast(_Msg, State) -> {noreply, State}.

handle_info({task_done, _ImgId}, State = #{active := A, done := D}) ->
    {noreply, State#{active := A - 1, done := D + 1}};
handle_info(_Info, State) -> {noreply, State}.

terminate(_R, _S) -> ok.
code_change(_O, S, _E) -> {ok, S}.
\`\`\`

## Assignment Specification

Implement \`src/async_report_server.erl\` managing background computational reports without blocking client traffic:
1. \`start_link() -> {ok, Pid}\`:
   - Initializes with state \`#{in_flight => 0, completed => 0}\`.
2. \`generate_report(Pid, JobId, ComputeFun) -> {ok, JobId, Result}\`:
   - Synchronous call \`gen_server:call(Pid, {generate_report, JobId, ComputeFun}, 3000)\`.
   - In \`handle_call/3\`:
     - Spawns a background worker executing \`Result = ComputeFun()\`.
     - The worker invokes \`gen_server:reply(From, {ok, JobId, Result})\` directly to unblock the caller.
     - The worker informs the server via \`ServerPid ! {job_finished, JobId}\`.
     - Immediately returns \`{noreply, State#{in_flight := InFlight + 1}}\`.
3. \`handle_info({job_finished, _JobId}, State)\`:
   - Decrements \`in_flight - 1\` and increments \`completed + 1\`. Returns \`{noreply, NewState}\`.
4. \`get_completed_count(Pid) -> {ok, #{in_flight => non_neg_integer(), completed => non_neg_integer()}}\`:
   - Synchronous call returning the current in-flight and completed counters.
5. \`hibernate_idle(Pid) -> hibernated\`:
   - Calls \`gen_server:call(Pid, hibernate_now)\` whose \`handle_call\` returns \`{reply, hibernated, State, hibernate}\`.
6. \`stop(Pid) -> ok\`.

## Rules & Verification Constraints

- Must export \`start_link/0\`, \`generate_report/3\`, \`get_completed_count/1\`, \`hibernate_idle/1\`, and \`stop/1\`.

- Must support \`hibernate\` return tuple in \`hibernate_idle/1\`.

  {
    id: 'ch07-l05',

    title: 'gen_statem: Protocol & Circuit Breaker State Machines',
    difficulty: 'Production',
    conceptMarkdown: `## Why This Matters in Production

In Chapter 5 (Lesson 5.6), we modeled a stateful door lock actor using **mutual tail-recursion** (\`locked(Code, Attempts)\` $\leftrightarrow$ \`unlocked(Code)\`).
While manual tail-recursive state functions work well for small scripts, complex network protocols (such as TCP handshakes, TLS negotiation, and XMPP client-to-server connections) require tracking states, state timeouts, delayed events, and transitions across dozens of phases.

For production state machines, the OTP framework provides **\`gen_statem\`** (which replaced the legacy \`gen_fsm\` in OTP 19).

In modern cloud architectures, one of the most critical patterns implemented using \`gen_statem\` is the **Circuit Breaker**:
- When downstream external services (payment APIs, database clusters, third-party auth) experience outages, naive callers keep hammering them with retries, making the outage worse and exhausting connection pools.
- A **Circuit Breaker** sits between your backend and the remote service. If calls fail repeatedly, it "trips" into an \`open\` state that **immediately fast-fails all subsequent calls in 0ms without contacting the network**!
- After an idle cooldown timeout, it transitions to \`half_open\` to test a single trial request. If successful, it automatically heals back to \`closed\`!

## Deep Concept Breakdown & Under the Hood

### The \`state_functions\` Callback Mode

A \`gen_statem\` can operate in two modes declared via \`callback_mode/0\`:
1. \`handle_event_function\`: A single callback handles all states.
2. **\`state_functions\` (Recommended & Idiomatic)**: Each state in your state machine is represented by **its own exported function of arity 3**:
   \`\`\`erlang
   StateName(EventType, EventContent, Data) ->
       {next_state, NextStateName, NewData} |
       {keep_state, NewData} |
       {keep_state, NewData, Actions}
   \`\`\`

### Event Types & State Machine Actions

Inside your state functions, \`EventType\` can be:
- \`{call, From}\`: Synchronous request initiated by \`gen_statem:call(Pid, Msg)\`. To reply, return action \`[{reply, From, Reply}]\`.
- \`cast\`: Asynchronous cast from \`gen_statem:cast(Pid, Msg)\`.
- \`info\`: Raw process messages (timers, monitors).
- **\`state_timeout\`**: A built-in timer attached strictly to the current state.

### Automated Timer Cancellation via \`state_timeout\`

When transitioning states, you can attach a state timeout action:
\`\`\`erlang
{next_state, open, NewData, [{state_timeout, 5000, try_half_open}]}
\`\`\`
The beauty of \`state_timeout\` is that **it automatically cancels itself** if the state machine leaves that state before the timer expires! You never have to manually track or cancel timer references.

### Circuit Breaker State Transition Matrix

| Current State | Event Received | Resulting Action | Next State |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **\`closed\`** | \`execute(Fun)\` succeeds | Return \`{ok, Res}\`; reset failure count to 0. | \`closed\` |
| **\`closed\`** | \`execute(Fun)\` fails (Failures < MaxFailures) | Return \`{error, Reason}\`; increment failures. | \`closed\` |
| **\`closed\`** | \`execute(Fun)\` fails (Failures >= MaxFailures) | Return \`{error, Reason}\`; arm \`state_timeout\`. | **\`open\`** |
| **\`open\`** | \`execute(Fun)\` | Fast-fail immediately with \`{error, circuit_open}\` (Do NOT run \`Fun\`!). | \`open\` |
| **\`open\`** | \`state_timeout\` fires | Transition to probe mode. | **\`half_open\`** |
| **\`half_open\`** | Trial \`execute(Fun)\` succeeds | Return \`{ok, Res}\`; reset failures to 0. | **\`closed\`** |
| **\`half_open\`** | Trial \`execute(Fun)\` fails | Return \`{error, Reason}\`; re-arm timeout. | **\`open\`** |

> [!warning] Production OTP Trap: State Timeout Cancellation Invariants
> Remember that \`{state_timeout, Ms, Event}\` is tied strictly to the state name. If your state machine executes an internal transition from \`open\` to \`open\` (e.g. \`{next_state, open, NewData}\`), the state timeout is **reset**! If you want to keep the existing running timer while updating state data, you must return \`{keep_state, NewData}\` instead of \`{next_state, CurrentState, NewData}\`.

## Parallel Worked Example

The following is an abbreviated 2-state toggle switch demonstrating \`gen_statem\` with \`state_functions\`:

\`\`\`erlang
-module(toggle_statem).
-behaviour(gen_statem).
-export([start_link/0, press/1, get_state/1, stop/1]).
-export([callback_mode/0, init/1, terminate/3, code_change/4]).
-export([off/3, on/3]).

callback_mode() -> state_functions.
start_link() -> gen_statem:start_link(?MODULE, [], []).
press(Pid) -> gen_statem:call(Pid, press).
get_state(Pid) -> gen_statem:call(Pid, get_state).
stop(Pid) -> gen_statem:stop(Pid).

init([]) -> {ok, off, #{presses => 0}}.

off({call, From}, press, Data = #{presses := P}) ->
    {next_state, on, Data#{presses := P + 1}, [{reply, From, switched_on}]};
off({call, From}, get_state, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, off}]}.

on({call, From}, press, Data = #{presses := P}) ->
    {next_state, off, Data#{presses := P + 1}, [{reply, From, switched_off}]};
on({call, From}, get_state, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, on}]}.

terminate(_R, _State, _Data) -> ok.
code_change(_Old, State, Data, _Extra) -> {ok, State, Data}.
\`\`\`

## Assignment Specification

Implement \`src/circuit_breaker_statem.erl\` representing a self-healing circuit breaker:
1. \`callback_mode() -> state_functions\`.
2. \`start_link(FailureThreshold, OpenTimeoutMs) -> {ok, Pid}\`:
   - Initial state is \`closed\`. Initial data is \`#{threshold => FailureThreshold, timeout => OpenTimeoutMs, failures => 0}\`.
3. \`execute(Pid, ActionFun)\`:
   - In \`closed\`:
     - Calls \`ActionFun()\`. If it returns \`{ok, Val}\`, resets \`failures => 0\` and replies \`{ok, Val}\`.
     - If it returns \`{error, Reason}\` or crashes, increments \`failures\`. If \`failures + 1 >= Threshold\`, transitions to \`open\` with action \`[{state_timeout, OpenTimeoutMs, try_half_open}]\` and replies \`{error, Reason}\`.
   - In \`open\`:
     - **Fast-fails immediately without running \`ActionFun()\`**, replying \`{error, circuit_open}\`.
     - When \`state_timeout\` event \`try_half_open\` triggers, transitions to \`half_open\`.
   - In \`half_open\`:
     - Executes \`ActionFun()\`. If \`{ok, Val}\`, transitions back to \`closed\` with \`failures => 0\` and replies \`{ok, Val}\`.
     - If \`{error, Reason}\`, trips back to \`open\` with \`state_timeout\` and replies \`{error, Reason}\`.
4. \`get_state_name(Pid) -> closed | open | half_open\`.
5. \`stop(Pid) -> ok\`.

## Rules & Verification Constraints

- Must implement \`-behaviour(gen_statem).\` and export \`callback_mode/0\`.
- Must export state functions \`closed/3\`, \`open/3\`, and \`half_open/3\`.
- In \`open\` state, must never invoke \`ActionFun()\`.

    starterCode: `-module(circuit_breaker_statem).
-behaviour(gen_statem).

-export([
    start_link/2,
    execute/2,
    get_state_name/1,

]).

%% gen_statem Callbacks
-export([
    callback_mode/0,
    init/1,
    closed/3,
    open/3,
    half_open/3,
    terminate/3,
    code_change/4
]).

%% Client API
start_link(FailureThreshold, OpenTimeoutMs) ->
    gen_statem:start_link(?MODULE, {FailureThreshold, OpenTimeoutMs}, []).

execute(Pid, ActionFun) when is_function(ActionFun, 0) ->
    ok.

get_state_name(Pid) ->
    closed.

stop(Pid) ->
    gen_statem:stop(Pid).

%% gen_statem Callbacks
callback_mode() ->
    state_functions.

init({Threshold, TimeoutMs}) ->
    Data = #{threshold => Threshold, timeout => TimeoutMs, failures => 0},
    {ok, closed, Data}.

closed({call, From}, get_state_name, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, closed}]};
closed({call, From}, _Msg, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, ok}]}.

open({call, From}, get_state_name, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, open}]};
open({call, From}, _Msg, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, {error, circuit_open}}]};
open(state_timeout, _Event, Data) ->
    {next_state, half_open, Data}.

half_open({call, From}, get_state_name, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, half_open}]};
half_open({call, From}, _Msg, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, ok}]}.

terminate(_Reason, _State, _Data) ->
    ok.

code_change(_OldVsn, State, Data, _Extra) ->
    {ok, State, Data}.

    solutionCode: `-module(circuit_breaker_statem).
-behaviour(gen_statem).

-export([
    start_link/2,
    execute/2,
    get_state_name/1,
    stop/1
]).

%% gen_statem Callbacks
-export([
    callback_mode/0,
    init/1,
    closed/3,
    open/3,
    half_open/3,
    terminate/3,
    code_change/4
]).

%% Client API
start_link(FailureThreshold, OpenTimeoutMs) ->
    gen_statem:start_link(?MODULE, {FailureThreshold, OpenTimeoutMs}, []).

execute(Pid, ActionFun) when is_function(ActionFun, 0) ->
    gen_statem:call(Pid, {execute, ActionFun}).

get_state_name(Pid) ->
    gen_statem:call(Pid, get_state_name).

stop(Pid) ->
    gen_statem:stop(Pid).

%% gen_statem Callbacks
callback_mode() ->
    state_functions.

init({Threshold, TimeoutMs}) ->
    Data = #{threshold => Threshold, timeout => TimeoutMs, failures => 0},
    {ok, closed, Data}.

%% ── Closed State ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
closed({call, From}, get_state_name, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, closed}]};
closed({call, From}, {execute, ActionFun}, Data = #{threshold := Threshold, timeout := TimeoutMs, failures := Failures}) ->
    case (try ActionFun() catch _:Crash -> {error, Crash} end) of
        {ok, Res} ->
            {keep_state, Data#{failures := 0}, [{reply, From, {ok, Res}}]};
        Err ->
            NewFailures = Failures + 1,
            if
                NewFailures >= Threshold ->
                    {next_state, open, Data#{failures := NewFailures}, [{state_timeout, TimeoutMs, try_half_open}, {reply, From, Err}]};
                true ->
                    {keep_state, Data#{failures := NewFailures}, [{reply, From, Err}]}
            end
    end.

%% ── Open State ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
open({call, From}, get_state_name, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, open}]};
open({call, From}, {execute, _ActionFun}, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, {error, circuit_open}}]};
open(state_timeout, try_half_open, Data) ->
    {next_state, half_open, Data}.

%% ── Half-Open State ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
half_open({call, From}, get_state_name, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, half_open}]};
half_open({call, From}, {execute, ActionFun}, Data = #{timeout := TimeoutMs}) ->
    case (try ActionFun() catch _:Crash -> {error, Crash} end) of
        {ok, Res} ->
            {next_state, closed, Data#{failures := 0}, [{reply, From, {ok, Res}}]};
        Err ->
            {next_state, open, Data, [{state_timeout, TimeoutMs, try_half_open}, {reply, From, Err}]}
    end.

terminate(_Reason, _State, _Data) ->
    ok.

code_change(_OldVsn, State, Data, _Extra) ->
    {ok, State, Data}.

    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, {error, circuit_open}}]};

    {next_state, half_open, Data}.

    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, half_open}]};

    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, ok}]}.

terminate(_Reason, _State, _Data) ->

execute(Pid, ActionFun) when is_function(ActionFun, 0) ->
    gen_statem:call(Pid, {execute, ActionFun}).

get_state_name(Pid) ->

stop(Pid) ->

%% gen_statem Callbacks
callback_mode() ->
    state_functions.

init({Threshold, TimeoutMs}) ->

%% ── Closed State ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
closed({call, From}, get_state_name, Data) ->
    {keep_state, Data, [{reply, From, closed}]};
closed({call, From}, {execute, ActionFun}, Data = #{threshold := Threshold, timeout := TimeoutMs, failures := Failures}) ->

        {ok, Res} ->
            {keep_state, Data#{failures := 0}, [{reply, From, {ok, Res}}]};

                    {keep_state, Data#{failures := NewFailures}, [{reply, From, Err}]}

  {
    id: 'ch07-l06',
    chapterNumber: 7,

    title: 'gen_event: Decoupled Event Buses & Security Audit Loggers',
    difficulty: 'Intermediate',
    conceptMarkdown: `## Why This Matters in Production

In microservices and high-throughput backends, decoupling event producers from consumers is essential for software evolution.
For example, when a user fails to log in:
- The security service wants to track failed attempts and trigger IP blocks.
- The compliance service wants to write an audit log to an immutable S3 bucket.
- The metrics service wants to increment a StatsD counter.

If the authentication service directly called three different \`gen_server\` processes for every login, it would create tight coupling: if the compliance server slowed down or crashed, the login pipeline would stall.

The OTP framework solves this with **\`gen_event\`**: a central event bus process that dispatches events to dynamically registered handler modules.

## Deep Concept Breakdown & Under the Hood

### The \`gen_event\` Architecture

Unlike a \`gen_server\` (which maps 1 process to 1 callback module), a \`gen_event\` architecture separates the **Event Manager process** from the **Handler modules**:
1. You start the manager process: \`{ok, ManagerPid} = gen_event:start_link()\`.
2. Different subsystems dynamically attach their callback handlers: \`gen_event:add_handler(ManagerPid, security_handler, Args)\`.
3. Producers broadcast events with **\`gen_event:notify(ManagerPid, Event)\`**.
4. The manager process iterates through all attached handlers, executing each handler's \`handle_event(Event, HandlerState)\` callback in order.

### Fault Isolation: What Happens When a Handler Crashes?

The most profound feature of \`gen_event\` is its resilience:
If handler A throws a runtime crash (e.g. \`badarith\` or network failure) during \`handle_event/2\`:
- **The Event Manager process does NOT crash!**
- Other handlers (B, C, and D) continue running unhurt!
- The manager simply catches the exception, logs a warning report, and automatically removes the broken handler A from its active handler list!

### Callback Signatures for \`gen_event\`

\`\`\`erlang
-module(my_handler).
-behaviour(gen_event).

init(Args) -> {ok, InitialState}.
handle_event(Event, State) -> {ok, NewState}.
handle_call(Query, State) -> {ok, Reply, NewState}.
handle_info(Info, State) -> {ok, NewState}.
terminate(Reason, State) -> ok.
code_change(OldVsn, State, Extra) -> {ok, NewState}.
\`\`\`

> [!warning] Production OTP Trap: Silent Removal of Crashing Event Handlers
> Because \`gen_event\` automatically unregisters handlers that crash without taking down the manager process, a bug in a handler can silently stop all event processing for that subsystem while your server appears completely healthy. In production, always monitor your SASL crash logs or use \`gen_event:add_sup_handler/3\` (which links the handler to the caller).

## Parallel Worked Example

The following is an audit event logger that tracks system warnings:

\`\`\`erlang
-module(warning_logger).
-behaviour(gen_event).
-export([add_handler/1, get_warnings/1]).
-export([init/1, handle_event/2, handle_call/2, handle_info/2, terminate/2, code_change/3]).

add_handler(Mgr) -> gen_event:add_handler(Mgr, ?MODULE, []).
get_warnings(Mgr) -> gen_event:call(Mgr, ?MODULE, get_warnings).

init([]) -> {ok, []}.

handle_event({warning, Msg}, Warnings) ->
    {ok, [Msg | Warnings]};
handle_event(_Other, Warnings) ->
    {ok, Warnings}.

handle_call(get_warnings, Warnings) ->
    {ok, lists:reverse(Warnings), Warnings}.

handle_info(_Info, State) -> {ok, State}.
terminate(_Reason, _State) -> ok.
code_change(_Old, State, _Extra) -> {ok, State}.
\`\`\`

## Assignment Specification

Implement \`src/security_audit_handler.erl\` tracking brute-force IP login attacks:
1. \`add_to_manager(ManagerPid, MaxAttempts) -> ok\`:
   - Attaches \`?MODULE\` to \`ManagerPid\` with initial state \`#{max => MaxAttempts, tracker => #{}}\`.
2. \`handle_event({login_failed, IpBinary}, State = #{max := Max, tracker := Tracker})\`:
   - Increments the failed attempt counter for \`IpBinary\`.
   - If \`NewCount >= Max\`, records \`alert => true\` for that IP.
   - Returns \`{ok, UpdatedState}\`.
3. \`handle_event({login_success, IpBinary}, State = #{tracker := Tracker})\`:
   - Clears previous failures for \`IpBinary\` (setting \`attempts => 0, alert => false\`).
   - Returns \`{ok, UpdatedState}\`.
4. \`get_ip_status(ManagerPid, IpBinary) -> {ok, #{attempts => non_neg_integer(), alert => boolean()}}\`:
   - Uses \`gen_event:call(ManagerPid, ?MODULE, {get_status, IpBinary})\`.
   - Replies with the status map for that IP (defaulting to \`attempts => 0, alert => false\` if IP was never seen).

## Rules & Verification Constraints

- Must export \`add_to_manager/2\` and \`get_ip_status/2\`.
- Must export all 6 mandatory \`gen_event\` callbacks.
- \`add_to_manager/2\` must use \`gen_event:add_handler/3\`.
- \`get_ip_status/2\` must use \`gen_event:call/3\`.
`,

    solutionCode: `-module(security_audit_handler).
-behaviour(gen_event).

-export([
    add_to_manager/2,
    get_ip_status/2
]).

%% gen_event Callbacks
-export([
    init/1,
    handle_event/2,
    handle_call/2,
    handle_info/2,
    terminate/2,
    code_change/3
]).

%% Client API
add_to_manager(ManagerPid, MaxAttempts) ->
    gen_event:add_handler(ManagerPid, ?MODULE, MaxAttempts).

get_ip_status(ManagerPid, IpBinary) ->
    gen_event:call(ManagerPid, ?MODULE, {get_status, IpBinary}).

%% gen_event Callbacks
init(MaxAttempts) ->
    {ok, #{max => MaxAttempts, tracker => #{}}}.

handle_event({login_failed, Ip}, State = #{max := Max, tracker := Tracker}) ->
    Current = maps:get(Ip, Tracker, #{attempts => 0, alert => false}),
    NewAttempts = maps:get(attempts, Current) + 1,
    Alert = NewAttempts >= Max,
    NewTracker = maps:put(Ip, #{attempts => NewAttempts, alert => Alert}, Tracker),
    {ok, State#{tracker := NewTracker}};

handle_event({login_success, Ip}, State = #{tracker := Tracker}) ->
    NewTracker = maps:put(Ip, #{attempts => 0, alert => false}, Tracker),
    {ok, State#{tracker := NewTracker}};

handle_event(_OtherEvent, State) ->
    {ok, State}.

handle_call({get_status, Ip}, State = #{tracker := Tracker}) ->
    Status = maps:get(Ip, Tracker, #{attempts => 0, alert => false}),
    {ok, {ok, Status}, State};
handle_call(_Req, State) ->
    {ok, {error, unknown_call}, State}.

handle_info(_Info, State) ->
    {ok, State}.

terminate(_Reason, _State) ->
    ok.

code_change(_OldVsn, State, _Extra) ->
    {ok, State}.

  // ── Lesson 7.7: Production Incident Triage Lab ────────────────────────────
  {
    id: 'ch07-l07',
    chapterNumber: 7,
    lessonNumber: 7,
    lessonType: 'incident_triage',
    title: 'Incident #103: Slow gen_server:init/1 Blocking Supervisor Startup',
    difficulty: 'Production',
    incidentAlert: {
      incidentId: 'INC-103',
      severity: 'CRITICAL',
      serviceName: 'firewall-rule-hydrator',
      symptom: 'During rolling deployments, the root supervisor times out and aborts boot whenever the firewall rule list exceeds 5,000 entries.',
      impact: 'Cluster nodes fail health checks and get killed by Kubernetes during rolling updates, causing service outages.',
      rootCauseHint: 'incident_blocking_init:init/1 performs synchronous rule compilation and normalization directly inside init/1 before returning {ok, State}, blocking gen_server:start_link/3.',
      fixObjective: 'Refactor init/1 to return {ok, #{status => booting, raw => SeedRules, rules => #{}}, {continue, {hydrate, SeedRules}}} immediately, and move rule compilation into handle_continue({hydrate, SeedRules}, State) setting status => ready.',
    },
    conceptMarkdown: `## 🚨 Incident Triage: Root Supervisor Boot Timeout (INC-103)

### Incident Context & Telemetry
At 03:14 UTC, during a routine zero-downtime rolling update of the security gateway cluster, Kubernetes pods running the \`firewall-rule-hydrator\` service failed their liveness probes.
The root OTP supervisor aborted startup with the following error log:

\`\`\`text
=CRASH REPORT====
  crasher:
    initial call: firewall_sup:init/1
    pid: <0.412.0>
    error: {shutdown, {failed_to_start_child, firewall_rules, timeout}}
\`\`\`

### Root-Cause Inspection
Inspecting \`src/incident_blocking_init.erl\` reveals that the server attempts to compile, normalize, and parse all firewall rules synchronously inside \`init/1\`:
\`\`\`erlang
%% BROKEN IMPLEMENTATION:
init(SeedRules) ->
    %% Heavy CPU loop compiling 5,000 rules blocks the caller for 6,200ms!
    CompiledMap = compile_all_rules(SeedRules),
    {ok, #{status => ready, rules => CompiledMap}}.
\`\`\`

Because \`gen_server:start_link/3\` blocks the parent supervisor until \`init/1\` returns, the supervisor reached its 5,000ms child startup timeout and killed the process!

### Your Fix Objective
Refactor \`incident_blocking_init.erl\` using the modern OTP 21+ **\`{continue, Term}\`** pattern:
1. \`init/1\` must return immediately in **< 1ms**:
   \`\`\`erlang
   {ok, #{status => booting, raw => SeedRules, rules => #{}}, {continue, {hydrate, SeedRules}}}
   \`\`\`
2. Move rule compilation into **\`handle_continue({hydrate, SeedRules}, State)\`**:
   - Compile \`SeedRules\` into the rules map: \`maps:from_list(SeedRules)\`.
   - Update internal state: \`State#{status := ready, rules := CompiledRules}\`.
   - Return \`{noreply, State}\`.
3. \`lookup_rule(Pid, Port)\`:
   - If \`status =:= ready\`, returns \`{ok, Action}\` if found, \`{error, not_found}\` otherwise.
   - If \`status =:= booting\`, returns \`{error, still_booting}\`.
4. Ensure \`get_status(Pid)\` returns \`ready\` after hydration completes.
`,
    mentalModelCheck: {
      question: 'Why does moving heavy startup logic into handle_continue/2 fix supervisor timeout crashes?',
      codeSnippet: `init(Rules) ->
    {ok, #{status => booting, rules => #{}}, {continue, {hydrate, Rules}}}.`,
      options: [
        {
          id: 'A',
          label: 'start_link returns {ok, Pid} to the supervisor immediately, allowing the supervisor to complete child registration while hydration proceeds without blocking boot.',
          isCorrect: true,
          explanation: 'Correct! The supervisor child registration completes in microseconds, preventing supervision timeouts during rolling releases.',

  {
    id: 'ch07-l08',
    chapterNumber: 7,
    lessonNumber: 8,

    title: 'Chapter 7 Problem Set: API Gateway Token-Bucket Rate Limiter (rate_limiter_srv.erl)',
    difficulty: 'Production',
    conceptMarkdown: `## Why This Matters in Production

In microservice ecosystems and public developer platforms (such as Stripe, GitHub, or AWS API Gateway), rate limiting is the primary defense line against distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, abusive web scrapers, and runaway client retry loops.

The gold standard for API throttling is the **Token-Bucket Algorithm**:
- Each client starts with a maximum bucket capacity of \`MaxTokens\`.
- Every incoming API request consumes $N$ tokens depending on its computational cost (e.g., \`GET /v1/user\` costs 1 token; heavy \`POST /v1/reports\` costs 5 tokens).
- If a client has sufficient tokens, the request is allowed immediately.
- If tokens are insufficient, the request is denied with an HTTP 429 status (\`{deny, Remaining}\`).
- Periodically, a background sweep refills $R$ tokens back into every active bucket, capped strictly at \`MaxTokens\`.

In this Capstone Problem Set for Chapter 7, you will engineer a high-throughput, production-grade **Token-Bucket Rate Limiter Server** using \`gen_server\`!

## Deep Concept Breakdown & Under the Hood

### State Architecture

Your \`gen_server\` maintains state as a map holding configuration, dynamic client balances, and global telemetry:

\`\`\`erlang
#{
    max_tokens => MaxTokens,         %% Maximum capacity per bucket (pos_integer())
    refill_amount => RefillAmount,   %% Tokens added per refill cycle (pos_integer())
    clients => #{                    %% Dynamic client token buckets (map())
        <<"client_1">> => 7,
        <<"client_2">> => 10
    },
    total_allowed => 0,              %% Global counter of approved requests (integer())
    total_rejected => 0              %% Global counter of rejected requests (integer())
}
\`\`\`

### Dynamic On-Demand Client Bucket Creation
When a request arrives for a previously unseen \`ClientId\`, your server must **automatically provision a fresh bucket with full \`MaxTokens\` capacity** before deducting the requested cost.

### Capped Batch Refills
When \`refill_all(Pid)\` is executed, every existing client bucket in \`clients\` receives \`RefillAmount\` additional tokens, capped at \`max_tokens\`:
\`\`\`erlang
NewTokens = min(CurrentTokens + RefillAmount, MaxTokens)
\`\`\`

### Live Introspection via \`sys:get_state/1\`
Because your module implements standard \`gen_server\` callbacks, production operators can inspect the exact internal balances and counters in real time using \`sys:get_state(Pid)\`!

> [!warning] Production OTP Trap: Map Allocation Leaks on Infinite Clients
> In a production gateway handling millions of ephemeral IP addresses, inserting an entry into \`clients\` for every unique IP will eventually exhaust memory. In production systems (as we will explore in Chapter 9), client buckets are backed by off-heap ETS tables with automatic TTL evictions (\`select_delete\`).

## Assignment Specification

Implement \`src/rate_limiter_srv.erl\` with the following exports:

\`\`\`erlang
-module(rate_limiter_srv).
-behaviour(gen_server).

-export([
    start_link/2,
    check_request/3,
    refill_all/1,
    reset_client/2,
    get_stats/1,
    stop/1
]).
\`\`\`

1. \`start_link(MaxTokens, RefillAmount) -> {ok, Pid}\`:
   - Spawns and links the \`gen_server\`. Initial state:
     \`#{max_tokens => MaxTokens, refill_amount => RefillAmount, clients => #{}, total_allowed => 0, total_rejected => 0}\`.
2. \`check_request(Pid, ClientId, Cost) -> {allow, Remaining} | {deny, Remaining}\`:
   - Synchronous \`call\`.
   - If \`ClientId\` is new, initial balance is \`MaxTokens\`.
   - If \`Balance >= Cost\`:
     - Decrements balance by \`Cost\`.
     - Increments \`total_allowed + 1\`.
     - Returns \`{allow, NewBalance}\`.
   - If \`Balance < Cost\`:
     - Balance remains unchanged.
     - Increments \`total_rejected + 1\`.
     - Returns \`{deny, Balance}\`.
3. \`refill_all(Pid) -> ok\`:
   - Synchronous \`call\` (or \`cast\`).
   - For every entry in \`clients\`, updates tokens to \`min(Tokens + RefillAmount, MaxTokens)\`. Returns \`ok\`.
4. \`reset_client(Pid, ClientId) -> ok\`:
   - Asynchronous \`cast\`. Resets \`ClientId\`'s balance directly to full \`MaxTokens\`. Returns \`ok\`.
5. \`get_stats(Pid) -> #{total_allowed => integer(), total_rejected => integer(), active_clients => integer()}\`:
   - Synchronous \`call\` returning aggregate metrics. \`active_clients\` is the number of keys in \`clients\`.
6. \`stop(Pid) -> ok\`:
   - Stops the server gracefully via \`gen_server:stop(Pid)\`.

## Rules & Verification Constraints

- Must export \`start_link/2\`, \`check_request/3\`, \`refill_all/1\`, \`reset_client/2\`, \`get_stats/1\`, and \`stop/1\`.
- Must export all 6 mandatory \`gen_server\` callbacks.
- \`reset_client/2\` must use \`gen_server:cast/2\`.
- \`check_request/3\` and \`get_stats/1\` must use \`gen_server:call/2\`.
- Token balances must never exceed \`MaxTokens\`.
`,

    solutionCode: `-module(rate_limiter_srv).
-behaviour(gen_server).

-export([
    start_link/2,
    check_request/3,
    refill_all/1,
    reset_client/2,
    get_stats/1,
    stop/1
]).

%% gen_server Callbacks
-export([
    init/1,
    handle_call/3,
    handle_cast/2,
    handle_info/2,
    terminate/2,
    code_change/3
]).

%% Client API
start_link(MaxTokens, RefillAmount) when is_integer(MaxTokens), is_integer(RefillAmount) ->
    gen_server:start_link(?MODULE, {MaxTokens, RefillAmount}, []).

check_request(Pid, ClientId, Cost) when is_integer(Cost), Cost > 0 ->
    gen_server:call(Pid, {check_request, ClientId, Cost}).

refill_all(Pid) ->
    gen_server:call(Pid, refill_all).

reset_client(Pid, ClientId) ->
    gen_server:cast(Pid, {reset_client, ClientId}).

get_stats(Pid) ->
    gen_server:call(Pid, get_stats).

stop(Pid) ->
    gen_server:stop(Pid).

%% gen_server Callbacks
init({MaxTokens, RefillAmount}) ->
    State = #{
        max_tokens => MaxTokens,
        refill_amount => RefillAmount,
        clients => #{},
        total_allowed => 0,
        total_rejected => 0
    },
    {ok, State}.

handle_call({check_request, ClientId, Cost}, _From, State = #{max_tokens := Max, clients := Clients, total_allowed := Allowed, total_rejected := Rejected}) ->
    CurrentTokens = maps:get(ClientId, Clients, Max),
    if
        CurrentTokens >= Cost ->
            Remaining = CurrentTokens - Cost,
            NewClients = maps:put(ClientId, Remaining, Clients),
            {reply, {allow, Remaining}, State#{clients := NewClients, total_allowed := Allowed + 1}};
        true ->
            {reply, {deny, CurrentTokens}, State#{total_rejected := Rejected + 1}}
    end;

handle_call(refill_all, _From, State = #{max_tokens := Max, refill_amount := Refill, clients := Clients}) ->
    RefilledClients = maps:map(fun(_Id, Tokens) ->
        min(Tokens + Refill, Max)
    end, Clients),
    {reply, ok, State#{clients := RefilledClients}};

handle_call(get_stats, _From, State = #{clients := Clients, total_allowed := Allowed, total_rejected := Rejected}) ->
    Stats = #{
        total_allowed => Allowed,
        total_rejected => Rejected,
        active_clients => maps:size(Clients)
    },
    {reply, Stats, State};

handle_call(_Req, _From, State) ->
    {reply, {error, unknown_call}, State}.

handle_cast({reset_client, ClientId}, State = #{max_tokens := Max, clients := Clients}) ->
    NewClients = maps:put(ClientId, Max, Clients),
    {noreply, State#{clients := NewClients}};
handle_cast(_Msg, State) ->
    {noreply, State}.

handle_info(_Info, State) ->
    {noreply, State}.

terminate(_Reason, _State) ->
    ok.

code_change(_OldVsn, State, _Extra) ->
    {ok, State}.

%% Client API

check_request(Pid, ClientId, Cost) when is_integer(Cost), Cost > 0 ->
    gen_server:call(Pid, {check_request, ClientId, Cost}).

refill_all(Pid) ->
    gen_server:call(Pid, refill_all).

reset_client(Pid, ClientId) ->
    gen_server:cast(Pid, {reset_client, ClientId}).

get_stats(Pid) ->
    gen_server:call(Pid, get_stats).

stop(Pid) ->
    gen_server:stop(Pid).

%% gen_server Callbacks
init({MaxTokens, RefillAmount}) ->
    State = #{
        max_tokens => MaxTokens,
        refill_amount => RefillAmount,
        clients => #{},
        total_allowed => 0,
        total_rejected => 0
    },
    {ok, State}.

handle_call({check_request, ClientId, Cost}, _From, State = #{max_tokens := Max, clients := Clients, total_allowed := Allowed, total_rejected := Rejected}) ->
    CurrentTokens = maps:get(ClientId, Clients, Max),
    if
        CurrentTokens >= Cost ->
            Remaining = CurrentTokens - Cost,
            NewClients = maps:put(ClientId, Remaining, Clients),
            {reply, {allow, Remaining}, State#{clients := NewClients, total_allowed := Allowed + 1}};
        true ->
            {reply, {deny, CurrentTokens}, State#{total_rejected := Rejected + 1}}
    end;

handle_call(refill_all, _From, State = #{max_tokens := Max, refill_amount := Refill, clients := Clients}) ->
    RefilledClients = maps:map(fun(_Id, Tokens) ->
        min(Tokens + Refill, Max)
    end, Clients),
    {reply, ok, State#{clients := RefilledClients}};

handle_call(get_stats, _From, State = #{clients := Clients, total_allowed := Allowed, total_rejected := Rejected}) ->
    Stats = #{
        total_allowed => Allowed,
        total_rejected => Rejected,
        active_clients => maps:size(Clients)
    },
    {reply, Stats, State};

handle_call(_Req, _From, State) ->
    {reply, {error, unknown_call}, State}.

handle_cast({reset_client, ClientId}, State = #{max_tokens := Max, clients := Clients}) ->
    NewClients = maps:put(ClientId, Max, Clients),
    {noreply, State#{clients := NewClients}};
handle_cast(_Msg, State) ->
    {noreply, State}.

handle_info(_Info, State) ->
    {noreply, State}.

terminate(_Reason, _State) ->
    ok.

code_change(_OldVsn, State, _Extra) ->
    {ok, State}.
`,

    difficulty: 'Intermediate',
    conceptMarkdown: `## Why This Matters in Production

In production backends, individual worker processes will inevitably encounter hardware timeouts, unexpected corrupt payloads, or database connection drops. The foundational architectural superpower of Erlang and the BEAM VM is **Supervision Trees** (\`-behaviour(supervisor).\`).

Instead of writing defensive \`try/catch\` blocks around every statement, Erlang systems embrace the **"Let It Crash"** philosophy:
1. **Workers** execute risky business logic. When unexpected corruption occurs, the worker crashes immediately, destroying its tainted heap.
2. **Supervisors** execute zero business logic. They exist solely to monitor workers and restore them to a known-clean state.

However, restoring workers requires choosing the correct **Restart Strategy**. If an independent caching worker crashes, you must not take down the entire system. Conversely, if a shared database connection crashes, downstream workers that depend on it must be cleanly restarted so they do not operate on dead handles.

### The 4 OTP Restart Strategies

1. **\`one_for_one\` (Independent Workers):**
   - If a child process terminates, only that single child is restarted.
   - Siblings are completely unaffected.
   - *Ideal for:* Independent web request handlers, stateless calculators, isolated worker pools.

2. **\`rest_for_one\` (Sequential Dependency Pipeline):**
   - If a child process terminates, any child process started **after** it in the specification list is terminated in reverse order and restarted in forward order.
   - Preceding upstream children are completely untouched!
   - *Ideal for:* Pipeline architectures like \`[db_pool -> pricing_cache -> order_gateway]\`. If \`pricing_cache\` crashes, \`order_gateway\` restarts, but \`db_pool\` remains online.

3. **\`one_for_all\` (Tightly Coupled Cluster):**
   - If any child process terminates, **all** other child processes are immediately terminated and restarted together.
   - *Ideal for:* Mutually dependent peers, such as a protocol worker and its companion active state monitor where neither can function without the other.

4. **\`simple_one_for_one\` (Dynamic Worker Factory):**
   - A supervisor that manages a dynamic pool of identical workers spawned on demand (e.g. active TCP sockets or incoming chat sessions).
   - Holds a single template child spec and starts with zero children at boot.

### The Modern Map-Based \`sup_flags()\` Format

In modern Erlang/OTP, the supervisor callback \`init/1\` returns:

\`\`\`erlang
{ok, {SupFlagsMap, [ChildSpecMap1, ChildSpecMap2, ...]}}
\`\`\`

The \`SupFlagsMap\` specifies how the supervisor handles child failures:

\`\`\`erlang
#{
    strategy => Strategy,    %% one_for_one | rest_for_one | one_for_all | simple_one_for_one
    intensity => Intensity,  %% Max allowable crashes (e.g., 3)
    period => Period         %% Sliding time window in seconds (e.g., 5)
}
\`\`\`

> [!warning] Production Supervision Trap: Infinite Crash Loops
> If a child process has a fatal initialization bug (e.g., invalid database credentials), the supervisor could blindly restart it billions of times, consuming 100% CPU and filling disk logs in seconds.
> The \`intensity\` (MaxRestarts) and \`period\` (MaxSeconds) parameters define a restart rate limit:
> - If more than \`Intensity\` crashes occur within \`Period\` seconds, the supervisor concludes that the subsystem is unrecoverable.
> - It terminates all surviving children in reverse startup order and terminates itself with \`shutdown\`!
> - This escalates the failure up to the parent supervisor in the tree.

### Parallel Worked Example

Here is how a telecom supervisor configures its strategies and calculates its restart budget:

\`\`\`erlang
-module(telecom_sup_planner).
-export([make_flags/3, route_strategy/1, eval_budget/2]).

make_flags(Strategy, MaxR, MaxT)
  when (Strategy =:= one_for_one orelse Strategy =:= rest_for_one orelse
        Strategy =:= one_for_all orelse Strategy =:= simple_one_for_one),
       is_integer(MaxR), MaxR >= 0,
       is_integer(MaxT), MaxT > 0 ->
    #{
        strategy => Strategy,
        intensity => MaxR,
        period => MaxT
    }.

route_strategy(independent_radios) -> one_for_one;
route_strategy(signal_pipeline)    -> rest_for_one;
route_strategy(dual_transceivers)  -> one_for_all;
route_strategy(dynamic_calls)      -> simple_one_for_one;
route_strategy(_)                  -> {error, unknown_topology}.

eval_budget(Crashes, Seconds)
  when is_integer(Crashes), is_integer(Seconds), Crashes >= 0, Seconds > 0 ->
    Rate = Crashes / Seconds,
    #{
        intensity => Crashes,
        period => Seconds,
        max_rate_per_sec => Rate,
        tolerated_downtime => ok
    }.
\`\`\`

### Your Mission

Implement module \`strategy_planner\` exporting:
1. \`build_sup_flags(Strategy, Intensity, Period) -> map()\`:
   - Validates that \`Strategy\` is one of \`[one_for_one, rest_for_one, one_for_all, simple_one_for_one]\`.
   - Validates that \`Intensity >= 0\` and \`Period > 0\`.
   - Returns the standardized \`#{strategy => Strategy, intensity => Intensity, period => Period}\` map.

3. \`calculate_restart_budget(MaxCrashes, WindowSeconds) -> map()\`:

   - Calculates \`Rate = MaxCrashes / WindowSeconds\`.
   - Returns \`#{intensity => MaxCrashes, period => WindowSeconds, max_rate_per_sec => Rate, tolerated_downtime => ok}\`.
`,

    visualScene: 'supervision_rest_for_one_ets_heir',
    difficulty: 'Intermediate',
    conceptMarkdown: `## Why This Matters in Production

A supervisor does not spawn processes randomly. Every process supervised by an OTP supervisor is defined by a **Child Specification** (\`child_spec()\`).

The child specification tells the supervisor:
1. What the child is named (\`id\`).
2. How to start it (\`start => {M, F, A}\`).
3. Under what conditions to restart it (\`restart\`).
4. How long to wait before forcefully killing it (\`shutdown\`).
5. Whether it is a leaf worker or an intermediate supervisor (\`type\`).
6. What modules to purge during dynamic code hot-reloading (\`modules\`).

### The Modern Map-Based \`child_spec()\` Anatomy

\`\`\`erlang
#{
    id => term(),                        %% Unique identifier atom or tuple
    start => {module(), atom(), list()}, %% {M, F, A} invocation returning {ok, Pid}
    restart => restart_type(),           %% permanent | transient | temporary
    shutdown => shutdown_timeout(),      %% brutal_kill | integer() ms | infinity
    type => worker | supervisor,         %% Declares node role in the hierarchy
    modules => [module()] | dynamic      %% Modules used for release packaging
}
\`\`\`

### The Restart Type Truth Table

The \`restart\` field defines the contract between process death reasons and restart behavior:

| Restart Type | Crash (\`error\`, \`badmatch\`, \`exit(crash)\`) | Normal Exit (\`exit(normal)\`) | Clean Shutdown (\`shutdown\`, \`{shutdown, Term}\`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **\`permanent\`** | **Restart** | **Restart** | **Restart** |
| **\`transient\`** | **Restart** | *Do NOT restart* | *Do NOT restart* |
| **\`temporary\`** | *Do NOT restart* | *Do NOT restart* | *Do NOT restart* |

- **\`permanent\`**: The process must NEVER be down (e.g. database connection pools, core message routers, listening sockets). Even if it exits with \`normal\`, the supervisor restarts it!
- **\`transient\`**: The process represents a task that eventually finishes cleanly (e.g. a batch file processor, an account registration pipeline). If it crashes unexpectedly, it is restarted; if it completes its job and exits \`normal\`, the supervisor lets it stay stopped.
- **\`temporary\`**: The process is disposable (e.g. dynamic client TCP sessions, rate-limit buckets). If it dies for *any* reason, it is never restarted.

### Shutdown Order & Timeouts

When a supervisor shuts down, or when \`rest_for_one\` / \`one_for_all\` restarts multiple children:
1. **Startup is strictly forward (top-to-bottom):** \`[Child1, Child2, Child3]\`.
2. **Shutdown is strictly reverse order:** \`Child3\` is terminated first, then \`Child2\`, then \`Child1\`.
3. To terminate a child, the supervisor sends an exit signal: \`exit(ChildPid, shutdown)\`.
4. If the child traps exits (\`process_flag(trap_exit, true)\`), it invokes its \`terminate(shutdown, State)\` callback to flush buffers and close sockets.
5. If the child does not exit within the specified \`shutdown\` milliseconds, the supervisor forcefully terminates it with \`exit(ChildPid, kill)\`.

> [!warning] Production Supervision Trap: Premature Killing of Child Supervisors
> For nested child supervisors, \`shutdown\` **MUST** be set to \`infinity\`!
> A child supervisor needs time to terminate all of its own children in reverse order before it can terminate itself. If a parent supervisor terminates a child supervisor with a 5,000ms timeout or \`brutal_kill\`, orphaned grandchild worker processes will leak into the BEAM VM.

### Parallel Worked Example

\`\`\`erlang
-module(worker_spec_builder).
-export([build_task_spec/4, build_sub_supervisor_spec/2, should_restart/2]).

build_task_spec(Id, Mod, Args, Restart)
  when is_atom(Mod), is_list(Args),
       (Restart =:= permanent orelse Restart =:= transient orelse Restart =:= temporary) ->
    #{
        id => Id,
        start => {Mod, start_link, Args},
        restart => Restart,
        shutdown => 5000,
        type => worker,
        modules => [Mod]
    }.

build_sub_supervisor_spec(Id, SupMod) when is_atom(SupMod) ->
    #{
        id => Id,
        start => {SupMod, start_link, []},
        restart => permanent,
        shutdown => infinity,  %% Mandatory for nested supervisors!
        type => supervisor,
        modules => [SupMod]
    }.

should_restart(permanent, _Reason) -> restart;
should_restart(temporary, _Reason) -> do_not_restart;
should_restart(transient, normal) -> do_not_restart;
should_restart(transient, shutdown) -> do_not_restart;
should_restart(transient, {shutdown, _}) -> do_not_restart;
should_restart(transient, _Abnormal) -> restart.
\`\`\`

### Your Mission

Implement module \`child_spec_factory\` exporting:
1. \`worker_spec(Id, Module, Args, RestartType) -> map()\`:
   - Validates that \`Module\` is an atom, \`Args\` is a list, and \`RestartType\` is \`permanent\`, \`transient\`, or \`temporary\`.
   - Returns a child spec map with \`start => {Module, start_link, Args}\`, \`shutdown => 5000\`, \`type => worker\`, and \`modules => [Module]\`.
2. \`supervisor_spec(Id, SupModule) -> map()\`:
   - Validates that \`SupModule\` is an atom.
   - Returns a child spec map with \`start => {SupModule, start_link, []}\`, \`restart => permanent\`, \`shutdown => infinity\`, \`type => supervisor\`, and \`modules => [SupModule]\`.
3. \`classify_restart(RestartType, ExitReason) -> restart | do_not_restart\`:
   - Implements the exact OTP Restart Type Truth Table.
`,

  {
    id: 'ch08-l03',
    chapterNumber: 8,
    lessonNumber: 3,
    lessonType: 'concept_exercise',
    title: 'Restart Intensity Blizzards (intensity/period) & Upward Crash Escalation',
    visualScene: 'supervision_rest_for_one_ets_heir',
    difficulty: 'Advanced',
    conceptMarkdown: `## Why This Matters in Production

What happens when a fatal dependency goes down—for instance, when the primary PostgreSQL database suffers a network partition, or a configuration file is corrupt?

If a \`permanent\` worker crashes immediately every time the supervisor starts it, what prevents the supervisor from spinning in an infinite 100% CPU restart loop that freezes the entire BEAM node?

### The OTP Sliding Window Rate Limiter

Every OTP supervisor implements an internal sliding window algorithm specified by two parameters in \`sup_flags()\`:
- **\`intensity => MaxR\`**: The maximum number of allowable crashes.
- **\`period => MaxT\`**: The sliding time window in seconds.

Whenever any child process terminates abnormally:
1. The supervisor records the current monotonic timestamp in its internal \`restarts\` queue.
2. It discards all recorded timestamps that are older than \`MaxT\` seconds relative to the latest crash.
3. It counts the number of crashes that occurred within the window \`[Latest - MaxT, Latest]\`.
4. **The Decision Point:**
   - If \`CrashCount <= MaxR\`: The supervisor stays within its restart budget. It restarts the child according to its strategy (\`one_for_one\`, \`rest_for_one\`, etc.).
   - If \`CrashCount > MaxR\`: The supervisor declares **Max Restart Intensity Exceeded**!

### The Upward Crash Escalation Cascade

When the restart intensity budget is exceeded:
1. The supervisor stops attempting to restart children. It recognizes that the problem is systemic and cannot be solved locally.
2. It terminates all of its surviving children in **strict reverse order** of startup.
3. It terminates **itself** with reason \`shutdown\`!
4. Because the supervisor is linked to its parent supervisor, its own termination triggers an exit signal up the supervision tree.
5. The parent supervisor now handles the failure—either restarting this entire subsystem or escalating further up to the root supervisor of the application release!

### Downstream Shutdown Order in \`rest_for_one\`

In a \`rest_for_one\` supervision tree with children \`[db_pool, pricing_cache, order_gateway]\`:
- If \`pricing_cache\` crashes, the affected children are \`[pricing_cache, order_gateway]\`.
- **Termination Order:** Downstream children must be stopped in **strict reverse order**: \`order_gateway\` is stopped first, then \`pricing_cache\`.
- **Restart Order:** They are restarted in **forward dependency order**: \`pricing_cache\` is restarted first, then \`order_gateway\`!
- The upstream dependency \`db_pool\` remains untouched.

> [!warning] Production Supervision Trap: Intensity Blizzard CPU Starvation
> Setting \`intensity => 1000, period => 1\` effectively disables crash throttling. If a bug causes an immediate crash on boot, the BEAM VM will spend 100% of its CPU cycles in supervisor loops, starving other schedulers. Always choose sensible values (e.g. \`intensity => 3..5, period => 5..10\`).

### Parallel Worked Example

\`\`\`erlang
-module(crash_escalator_demo).
-export([check_window/3, downstream_order/2]).

check_window([], _MaxR, _MaxT) ->
    {ok, within_budget};
check_window(Timestamps, MaxR, MaxT) ->
    Latest = lists:max(Timestamps),
    Cutoff = Latest - MaxT,
    Recent = [T || T <- Timestamps, T >= Cutoff, T =< Latest],
    case length(Recent) > MaxR of
        true -> {escalate, length(Recent), MaxR};
        false -> {ok, length(Recent), MaxR}
    end.

downstream_order(AllChildren, TargetId) ->
    case lists:splitwith(fun(Id) -> Id =/= TargetId end, AllChildren) of
        {_Prefix, []} -> {error, not_found};
        {_Prefix, Affected} ->
            {reverse_stop, lists:reverse(Affected), forward_restart, Affected}
    end.
\`\`\`

### Your Mission

Implement module \`escalation_analyzer\` exporting:
1. \`evaluate_crash_burst(CrashTimestampsSecList, MaxR, MaxT) -> {escalate_to_parent, Count, MaxR} | {within_budget, Count, MaxR}\`:
   - If list is empty, returns \`{within_budget, 0, MaxR}\`.
   - Finds \`Latest = lists:max(CrashTimestampsSecList)\`.
   - Counts timestamps \`Ts\` satisfying \`(Latest - MaxT) =< Ts andalso Ts =< Latest\`.
   - If \`Count > MaxR\`, returns \`{escalate_to_parent, Count, MaxR}\`; otherwise returns \`{within_budget, Count, MaxR}\`.
2. \`plan_escalation_action(ChildOrderList, CrashedChildId) -> {stop_in_reverse_order, ToStopReverseList, restart_in_order, ToRestartForwardList} | {error, child_not_found}\`:
   - Locates \`CrashedChildId\` in \`ChildOrderList\`. Returns \`{error, child_not_found}\` if missing.
   - Extracts the crashed child and all downstream children: \`Affected = [CrashedChildId | Downstream]\`.
   - Computes \`ToStopReverseList = lists:reverse(Affected)\`.
   - Computes \`ToRestartForwardList = Affected\`.
   - Returns \`{stop_in_reverse_order, ToStopReverseList, restart_in_order, ToRestartForwardList}\`.
3. \`reverse_shutdown_order(StartupChildIdsList) -> list()\`:
   - Returns \`lists:reverse(StartupChildIdsList)\`.
`,

    {within_budget, 0, MaxR};
evaluate_crash_burst(CrashTimestampsSecList, MaxR, MaxT)
  when is_list(CrashTimestampsSecList), is_integer(MaxR), MaxR >= 0, is_integer(MaxT), MaxT > 0 ->

        Count > MaxR -> {escalate_to_parent, Count, MaxR};

    end.

plan_escalation_action(ChildOrderList, CrashedChildId) when is_list(ChildOrderList) ->

            {error, child_not_found};

            ToStop = lists:reverse(Affected),
            ToRestart = Affected,
            {stop_in_reverse_order, ToStop, restart_in_order, ToRestart}
    end.

reverse_shutdown_order(StartupChildIdsList) when is_list(StartupChildIdsList) ->
    lists:reverse(StartupChildIdsList).

  // ── Lesson 8.4: Concept Exercise (Multi-File Clean Worker Architecture) ──
  {
    id: 'ch08-l04',
    chapterNumber: 8,
    lessonNumber: 4,
    lessonType: 'concept_exercise',
    title: 'Dynamic Worker Supervision (simple_one_for_one & supervisor:start_child)',
    visualScene: 'supervision_rest_for_one_ets_heir',
    difficulty: 'Intermediate',
    conceptMarkdown: `## Why This Matters in Production

Standard supervisors (\`one_for_one\`, \`rest_for_one\`) supervise a **static list of known children** declared at boot time.

However, modern systems frequently require **dynamic process pools**:
- A TCP server spawning a new worker process for every incoming connection.
- An XMPP server creating a dedicated state machine for every logged-in user session.
- A background job queue spawning workers on demand.

For this pattern, OTP provides the **\`simple_one_for_one\`** supervisor strategy.

### How \`simple_one_for_one\` Works

1. **Zero Children at Boot:** When \`dynamic_session_sup:start_link()\` runs, the supervisor starts with **zero** active children.
2. **Single Child Spec Template:** The \`init/1\` callback returns a list containing **exactly one** child specification template.
3. **Dynamic Spawning via \`supervisor:start_child/2\`:**
   - The template defines the starting MFA: \`start => {session_worker, start_link, []}\`.
   - When a caller invokes \`supervisor:start_child(SupRef, [SessionId, UserId])\`, the supervisor **appends** the arguments in the second parameter to the template's start MFA list!
   - This dynamically executes: \`session_worker:start_link(SessionId, UserId)\`.

### Eliminating the Mixed Supervisor/Worker Anti-Pattern

> [!warning] Production Supervision Trap: Overloading Supervisor init/1
> A common beginner mistake is cramming both \`-behaviour(supervisor).\` and \`-behaviour(gen_server).\` into the same file by overloading \`init/1\`:
> \`\`\`erlang
> %% ANTI-PATTERN: DO NOT DO THIS!
> init([]) -> {ok, {SupFlags, [Template]}};  %% Supervisor callback
> init({worker, SessionId}) -> {ok, State}.   %% Worker callback!
> \`\`\`
> This causes severe cognitive friction, mixes lifecycle management with business state, and breaks OTP tooling.
> **The Idiomatic OTP Architecture:**
> - File 1: \`src/dynamic_session_sup.erl\` (\`-behaviour(supervisor).\`)
> - File 2: \`src/session_worker.erl\` (\`-behaviour(gen_server).\`)

Look at the second tab in your editor: \`session_worker.erl\` is already written as a clean, separate \`gen_server\` worker. Your job is to implement the supervisor \`dynamic_session_sup.erl\`!

### Parallel Worked Example

\`\`\`erlang
-module(dynamic_pool_sup).
-behaviour(supervisor).
-export([start_link/0, add_worker/2, count_active/1, remove_worker/2, init/1]).

start_link() ->
    supervisor:start_link(?MODULE, []).

init([]) ->
    SupFlags = #{
        strategy => simple_one_for_one,
        intensity => 10,
        period => 5
    },
    ChildTemplate = #{
        id => pool_worker,
        start => {pool_worker, start_link, []},
        restart => temporary,
        shutdown => 2000,
        type => worker,
        modules => [pool_worker]
    },
    {ok, {SupFlags, [ChildTemplate]}}.

add_worker(SupRef, TaskId, Priority) ->
    supervisor:start_child(SupRef, [TaskId, Priority]).

count_active(SupRef) ->
    Counts = supervisor:count_children(SupRef),
    case is_map(Counts) of
        true  -> maps:get(active, Counts, 0);
        false -> proplists:get_value(active, Counts, 0)
    end.

remove_worker(SupRef, ChildPid) ->
    supervisor:terminate_child(SupRef, ChildPid).
\`\`\`

### Your Mission

Implement module \`dynamic_session_sup\` with \`-behaviour(supervisor).\` exporting:
1. \`start_link/0 -> {ok, pid()}\`:
   - Calls \`supervisor:start_link({local, ?MODULE}, ?MODULE, [])\`.
2. \`init([]) -> {ok, {SupFlags, [ChildTemplate]}}\`:
   - Returns \`SupFlags = #{strategy => simple_one_for_one, intensity => 10, period => 5}\`.
   - Returns a single \`ChildTemplate\` with \`id => session_worker\`, \`start => {session_worker, start_link, []}\`, \`restart => temporary\`, \`shutdown => 2000\`, \`type => worker\`, \`modules => [session_worker]\`.
3. \`start_session(SupRef, SessionId, UserId) -> {ok, pid()}\`:
   - Invokes \`supervisor:start_child(SupRef, [SessionId, UserId])\`.
4. \`count_sessions(SupRef) -> integer()\`:
   - Invokes \`supervisor:count_children(SupRef)\` and extracts the active child count.
5. \`terminate_session(SupRef, ChildPid) -> ok\`:
   - Invokes \`supervisor:terminate_child(SupRef, ChildPid)\`.
`,
    mentalModelCheck: {
      question: 'Why does simple_one_for_one allow only ONE child specification template inside init/1?',

    starterCode: `-module(dynamic_session_sup).
-behaviour(supervisor).

-export([
    start_link/0,

    init/1
]).

start_link() ->

init([]) ->

`,
    solutionCode: `-module(dynamic_session_sup).
-behaviour(supervisor).

-export([
    start_link/0,
    start_session/3,
    count_sessions/1,
    terminate_session/2,
    init/1
]).

start_link() ->
    supervisor:start_link({local, ?MODULE}, ?MODULE, []).

init([]) ->
    SupFlags = #{
        strategy => simple_one_for_one,
        intensity => 10,
        period => 5
    },
    ChildTemplate = #{
        id => session_worker,
        start => {session_worker, start_link, []},
        restart => temporary,
        shutdown => 2000,
        type => worker,
        modules => [session_worker]
    },
    {ok, {SupFlags, [ChildTemplate]}}.

start_session(SupRef, SessionId, UserId) ->
    supervisor:start_child(SupRef, [SessionId, UserId]).

count_sessions(SupRef) ->
    Counts = supervisor:count_children(SupRef),
    case is_map(Counts) of
        true  -> maps:get(active, Counts, 0);
        false ->
            case lists:keyfind(active, 1, Counts) of
                {active, N} -> N;
                false -> 0
            end

start_session(SupRef, SessionId, UserId) ->

count_sessions(SupRef) ->
    Counts = supervisor:count_children(SupRef),
    case is_map(Counts) of
        true  -> maps:get(active, Counts, 0);
        false ->
            case lists:keyfind(active, 1, Counts) of
                {active, N} -> N;
                false -> 0
            end
    end.

terminate_session(SupRef, ChildPid) ->
    supervisor:terminate_child(SupRef, ChildPid).

    conceptMarkdown: `## Why This Matters in Production

In Erlang/OTP, an **Application** is a self-contained component that can be started and stopped as a single unit, packaged into production releases, and configured at runtime.

Every production system you build—from an HTTP REST API to an XMPP cluster—is structured as one or more OTP applications.

### The Two Components of an OTP Application

1. **The Application Resource File (\`.app\` or \`.app.src\`):**
   - A declarative metadata file containing the application's name, version, registered names, dependencies, and configuration parameters.
   - Declares the callback module implementing \`-behaviour(application).\`.

2. **The Application Callback Module:**
   - Implements \`start(StartType, StartArgs) -> {ok, SupPid} | {error, Reason}\`.
   - Implements \`stop(State) -> ok\`.
   - The \`start/2\` callback is invoked by the BEAM **Application Master** process. It spawns the root supervisor of the application's supervision tree and returns the root supervisor's PID.

### The \`.app.src\` Resource Specification

\`\`\`erlang
{application, commerce_app, [
    {description, "E-Commerce Core Checkout & Order Engine"},
    {vsn, "1.0.0"},
    {registered, [commerce_app, checkout_sup]},
    {mod, {commerce_app, []}},
    {applications, [kernel, stdlib]},
    {env, [
        {currency, "USD"},
        {max_retries, 3},
        {checkout_timeout_ms, 5000}
    ]}
]}.
\`\`\`

### Runtime Configuration with \`application:get_env/3\`

Production code must NEVER hardcode configuration parameters (like API tokens, database hosts, or timeout thresholds).

OTP provides built-in application configuration management:
- **\`application:get_env(App, Key, Default)\`**: Reads the runtime configuration parameter for \`App\`. If unset, safely returns \`Default\`.
- **\`application:set_env(App, Key, Value)\`**: Updates the runtime configuration dynamically in the application controller.

> [!warning] Production Supervision Trap: Hardcoded Configuration Constants
> Never write \`Timeout = 5000\` inside worker processes. If production network conditions require increasing timeouts during high traffic, hardcoded values require recompilation and redeployment. Using \`application:get_env(my_app, timeout_ms, 5000)\` allows dynamic tuning via \`sys.config\` or live console RPC without downtime.

### Parallel Worked Example

\`\`\`erlang
-module(auth_app).
-behaviour(application).
-behaviour(supervisor).

-export([start/2, stop/1, get_config/2, set_config/2, init/1]).

start(_StartType, _StartArgs) ->
    case supervisor:start_link({local, ?MODULE}, ?MODULE, []) of
        {ok, SupPid} -> {ok, SupPid};
        {error, {already_started, SupPid}} -> {ok, SupPid};
        {error, Reason} -> {error, Reason}
    end.

stop(_State) ->
    ok.

get_config(Key, Default) ->
    application:get_env(auth_app, Key, Default).

set_config(Key, Value) ->
    application:set_env(auth_app, Key, Value).

init([]) ->
    SupFlags = #{
        strategy => one_for_one,
        intensity => 3,
        period => 5
    },
    ChildSpecs = [],
    {ok, {SupFlags, ChildSpecs}}.
\`\`\`

### Your Mission

Implement module \`commerce_app\` implementing both \`-behaviour(application).\` and \`-behaviour(supervisor).\`:
1. \`start(StartType, StartArgs) -> {ok, pid()} | {error, term()}\`:
   - Spawns the supervisor using \`supervisor:start_link({local, ?MODULE}, ?MODULE, [])\`.
   - Returns \`{ok, SupPid}\` (handles \`{error, {already_started, SupPid}}\` gracefully).
2. \`stop(State) -> ok\`:
   - Performs clean teardown; returns \`ok\`.
3. \`get_app_config(Key, Default) -> term()\`:
   - Invokes \`application:get_env(commerce_app, Key, Default)\`.
4. \`set_app_config(Key, Value) -> ok\`:
   - Invokes \`application:set_env(commerce_app, Key, Value)\`.
5. \`init([]) -> {ok, {SupFlags, ChildSpecs}}\`:
   - Returns \`strategy => one_for_one\`, \`intensity => 3\`, \`period => 5\`, and \`ChildSpecs = []\`.
`,

  // ── Lesson 8.6: Incident Triage (#104) ────────────────────────────────────
  {
    id: 'ch08-l06',
    chapterNumber: 8,
    lessonNumber: 6,
    lessonType: 'incident_triage',
    title: 'Incident #104: Misconfigured Supervision Strategy Leaving Stale Downstream Workers',
    visualScene: 'supervision_rest_for_one_ets_heir',
    difficulty: 'Advanced',
    incidentAlert: {
      incidentId: 'INC-104',
      severity: 'HIGH',
      serviceName: 'auth-pipeline-sup',
      symptom: 'When auth_cache crashes under memory pressure, it never restarts (leaving the cache dead), and downstream api_router continues running with broken references!',
      rootCauseHint: 'init/1 in incident_wrong_strategy.erl configured strategy => one_for_one instead of rest_for_one, set intensity => 0 (so the very first crash kills the supervisor!), and marked auth_cache as restart => temporary.',
      fixObjective: 'Fix init([]) to return strategy => rest_for_one, intensity => 5, period => 10, and ensure all 3 pipeline children ([worker_db, worker_cache, worker_http]) have restart => permanent and type => worker.',
      impact: 'Total failure of authentication routing when cache worker crashes.',
    },
    conceptMarkdown: `## Postmortem & Triage Lab: Incident #104

You are on call for the authentication gateway cluster. At 03:14 UTC, an alert triggered:

> **CRITICAL OUTAGE:** Authentication requests are failing with \`{error, bad_cache_pid}\`. Downstream \`api_router\` is logging thousands of dead process crashes, while the supervisor itself remains idle and the cache process is nowhere to be found!

### System Topology

The authentication subsystem is a sequential dependency pipeline:
\`\`\`
[worker_db] -> [worker_cache] -> [worker_http]
\`\`\`
1. \`worker_db\`: Manages the primary credentials database.
2. \`worker_cache\`: In-memory cache dependent on \`worker_db\`.
3. \`worker_http\`: External HTTP routing gateway dependent on \`worker_cache\`.

### Root Cause Analysis

Inspecting \`incident_wrong_strategy:init/1\` reveals three critical bugs:
1. **Wrong Strategy (\`one_for_one\`):** When \`worker_cache\` crashes, \`one_for_one\` ignores downstream \`worker_http\`. The HTTP gateway continues running, attempting to query a dead cache PID!
2. **Temporary Restart Policy (\`temporary\`):** \`worker_cache\` was marked \`restart => temporary\`! When it crashed under memory pressure, the supervisor never restarted it at all!
3. **Zero Restart Intensity (\`intensity => 0\`):** The supervisor configured \`intensity => 0\`, meaning if *any* process crashed, the supervisor would commit suicide immediately!

### Triage & Fix Objective

1. Update the restart strategy to **\`rest_for_one\`**.
2. Set **\`intensity => 5, period => 10\`** to tolerate transient blizzards.
3. Update all 3 child specifications to **\`restart => permanent\`**.
4. Keep \`shutdown => 2000\`, \`type => worker\`, and \`modules => [incident_wrong_strategy]\`.
`,
    mentalModelCheck: {
      question: 'Why is rest_for_one mandatory for [db -> cache -> http] pipelines instead of one_for_one?',
      options: [
        {
          id: 'A',
          label: 'Because when an upstream worker (like cache) restarts, downstream workers (like http) must be restarted to invalidate stale handles and reconnect to the new PID.',
          isCorrect: true,
          explanation: 'rest_for_one guarantees that any child dependent on an upstream worker is cleanly restarted in sequence.',
        },
        {
          id: 'B',
          label: 'Because one_for_one only allows two children total.',
          isCorrect: false,
          explanation: 'one_for_one allows any number of children, but restarts them in total isolation.',
        },
        {
          id: 'C',
          label: 'Because rest_for_one executes 10x faster than one_for_one.',
          isCorrect: false,
          explanation: 'Restart strategy choice is about architectural dependency correctness, not raw execution speed.',
        },
        {
          id: 'D',
          label: 'Because the Erlang compiler rejects one_for_one on pipelines.',
          isCorrect: false,
          explanation: 'The compiler cannot know your architectural dependencies; you must choose the correct strategy.',
        },
      ],
    },

        officialUrl: 'https://www.erlang.org/doc/apps/stdlib/supervisor.html#which_children/1',
      },
    ],
    starterCode: `-module(incident_wrong_strategy).
-behaviour(supervisor).

-export([
    start_link/0,
    init/1,
    build_pipeline_specs/0,
    audit_flags/0,
    test_chaos_cascade/0
]).
-export([worker_loop/1]).

start_link() ->
    supervisor:start_link(?MODULE, []).

init([]) ->
    %% BUGGY IMPLEMENTATION (INCIDENT #104):
    SupFlags = #{
        strategy => one_for_one,
        intensity => 0,
        period => 1
    },
    ChildSpecs = [
        #{
            id => worker_db,
            start => {incident_wrong_strategy, worker_loop, [db]},
            restart => temporary,
            shutdown => 2000,
            type => worker,
            modules => [incident_wrong_strategy]
        },
        #{
            id => worker_cache,
            start => {incident_wrong_strategy, worker_loop, [cache]},
            restart => temporary,
            shutdown => 2000,
            type => worker,
            modules => [incident_wrong_strategy]
        },
        #{
            id => worker_http,
            start => {incident_wrong_strategy, worker_loop, [http]},
            restart => temporary,
            shutdown => 2000,
            type => worker,
            modules => [incident_wrong_strategy]
        }
    ],
    {ok, {SupFlags, ChildSpecs}}.

build_pipeline_specs() ->
    {ok, {_SupFlags, ChildSpecs}} = init([]),
    ChildSpecs.

worker_loop(Role) ->
    Pid = spawn_link(fun() -> run_worker(Role) end),
    {ok, Pid}.

run_worker(Role) ->
    receive
        stop -> ok;
        _ -> run_worker(Role)
    end.

audit_flags() ->
    {ok, {SupFlags, ChildSpecs}} = init([]),
    Strategy = maps:get(strategy, SupFlags),
    Restarts = [maps:get(restart, Spec) || Spec <- ChildSpecs],
    {ok, Strategy, Restarts}.

test_chaos_cascade() ->
    {ok, Sup} = start_link(),
    Children1 = supervisor:which_children(Sup),
    {_, Db1, _, _} = lists:keyfind(worker_db, 1, Children1),
    {_, Cache1, _, _} = lists:keyfind(worker_cache, 1, Children1),
    {_, Http1, _, _} = lists:keyfind(worker_http, 1, Children1),
    exit(Cache1, kill),
    timer:sleep(50),
    Children2 = supervisor:which_children(Sup),
    {_, Db2, _, _} = lists:keyfind(worker_db, 1, Children2),
    {_, Cache2, _, _} = lists:keyfind(worker_cache, 1, Children2),
    {_, Http2, _, _} = lists:keyfind(worker_http, 1, Children2),
    exit(Sup, shutdown),
    case Db1 =:= Db2 andalso Cache1 =/= Cache2 andalso Http1 =/= Http2 of
        true -> {ok, db_unaffected, downstream_restarted};
        false -> {error, cascade_failed}
    end.
`,
    solutionCode: `-module(incident_wrong_strategy).
-behaviour(supervisor).

-export([
    start_link/0,
    init/1,
    build_pipeline_specs/0,
    audit_flags/0,
    test_chaos_cascade/0
]).
-export([worker_loop/1]).

start_link() ->
    supervisor:start_link(?MODULE, []).

init([]) ->
    SupFlags = #{
        strategy => rest_for_one,
        intensity => 5,
        period => 10
    },
    ChildSpecs = [
        #{
            id => worker_db,
            start => {incident_wrong_strategy, worker_loop, [db]},
            restart => permanent,
            shutdown => 2000,
            type => worker,
            modules => [incident_wrong_strategy]
        },
        #{
            id => worker_cache,
            start => {incident_wrong_strategy, worker_loop, [cache]},
            restart => permanent,
            shutdown => 2000,
            type => worker,
            modules => [incident_wrong_strategy]

            restart => permanent,

        true -> {ok, db_unaffected, downstream_restarted};

    difficulty: 'Advanced',
    conceptMarkdown: `## Architectural Mission: E-Commerce Checkout Pipeline

Welcome to the Chapter 8 Problem Set! You will architect a production-grade, fault-isolated **E-Commerce Checkout Supervision Tree**.

In real-world e-commerce backends, checkout pipelines consist of strictly ordered micro-services:
1. **\`db_pool\`**: Database connection pool maintaining long-lived TCP connections. Must remain stable at all costs.
2. **\`pricing_cache\`**: Fast in-memory caching worker dependent on \`db_pool\`.
3. **\`order_gateway\`**: Payment and order submission gateway dependent on \`pricing_cache\`.

### Architectural Requirements

1. **Strategy Selection:**
   - The supervision tree must use **\`rest_for_one\`** with **\`intensity => 5, period => 10\`**.
   - If \`order_gateway\` crashes, only \`order_gateway\` restarts. \`db_pool\` and \`pricing_cache\` are unaffected.
   - If \`pricing_cache\` crashes, \`pricing_cache\` and \`order_gateway\` restart in dependency order. \`db_pool\` is untouched.
   - If \`db_pool\` crashes, the entire pipeline is cleanly restarted in order.

2. **Strict Clean Worker Separation:**
   - Look at the second tab in your editor: \`src/checkout_worker.erl\` is already implemented as a clean, separate \`gen_server\` worker.
   - In \`src/checkout_sup.erl\`, configure each child spec with:
     - \`start => {checkout_worker, start_link, [RegisteredName, Role]}\`
     - Child 1: \`id => db_pool\`, \`start => {checkout_worker, start_link, [db_pool_worker, db]}\`
     - Child 2: \`id => pricing_cache\`, \`start => {checkout_worker, start_link, [pricing_cache_worker, cache]}\`
     - Child 3: \`id => order_gateway\`, \`start => {checkout_worker, start_link, [order_gateway_worker, gateway]}\`
     - All 3 children must have \`restart => permanent\`, \`shutdown => 5000\`, \`type => worker\`, and \`modules => [checkout_worker]\`.

3. **Pipeline PID Introspection (\`get_pipeline_pids/0\`):**
   - Calls \`supervisor:which_children(?MODULE)\`.
   - Locates each child by its ID tuple (or registered process fallback).
   - Returns \`{ok, #{db_pid => DbPid, cache_pid => CachePid, gateway_pid => GatewayPid}}\`.

### The 3-Stage Live Chaos Test

Your supervision tree will be subjected to automated chaos injection in the test suite:
- **Chaos 1:** \`order_gateway\` is killed with \`exit(kill)\`. Confirms ONLY Child 3 restarted; DB and Cache PIDs match their original values.
- **Chaos 2:** \`pricing_cache\` is killed with \`exit(kill)\`. Confirms Child 2 and Child 3 received NEW PIDs, while DB Pool PID is preserved!
- **Chaos 3:** \`db_pool\` is killed with \`exit(kill)\`. Confirms all 3 processes are restarted in sequence with new PIDs!
`,

-behaviour(supervisor).

]).

start_link() ->
    supervisor:start_link({local, ?MODULE}, ?MODULE, []).

init([]) ->
    SupFlags = #{
        strategy => rest_for_one,
        intensity => 5,
        period => 10
    },
    ChildSpecs = [
        #{
            id => db_pool,
            start => {checkout_worker, start_link, [db_pool_worker, db]},
            restart => permanent,
            shutdown => 5000,
            type => worker,
            modules => [checkout_worker]
        },
        #{
            id => pricing_cache,

            modules => [checkout_worker]
        }

    {ok, {SupFlags, ChildSpecs}}.

    Children = supervisor:which_children(?MODULE),
    DbPid = case lists:keyfind(db_pool, 1, Children) of
        {db_pool, P1, _, _} -> P1;
        _ -> whereis(db_pool_worker)
    end,
    CachePid = case lists:keyfind(pricing_cache, 1, Children) of
        {pricing_cache, P2, _, _} -> P2;
        _ -> whereis(pricing_cache_worker)

    GatewayPid = case lists:keyfind(order_gateway, 1, Children) of
        {order_gateway, P3, _, _} -> P3;
        _ -> whereis(order_gateway_worker)
    end,
    {ok, #{db_pid => DbPid, cache_pid => CachePid, gateway_pid => GatewayPid}}.

]).

start_link(RegName, Role) ->
    gen_server:start_link({local, RegName}, ?MODULE, Role, []).

init(Role) ->
    {ok, #{role => Role, restarts => 0}}.

get_role(Pid) ->
    gen_server:call(Pid, get_role).

handle_call(get_role, _From, #{role := Role} = State) ->
    {reply, {ok, Role}, State};
handle_call(_Req, _From, State) ->
    {reply, ok, State}.

handle_cast(_Msg, State) ->
    {noreply, State}.

handle_info(_Info, State) ->
    {noreply, State}.

terminate(_Reason, _State) ->
    ok.

code_change(_OldVsn, State, _Extra) ->
    {ok, State}.
`,
